passage: Week one. Karthik lay awake till three, running through it: what if he failed chemistry, what if the headache meant something serious, what if his friends were laughing at him in the group chat. At breakfast, when his sister Ganga asked for the salt, he snapped at her. Week four. It hadn't stopped. He'd dropped cricket practice because his mind wouldn't sit still long enough to bat. Ganga found him at midnight on the balcony, jaw tight. "It's every night, isn't it?" He nodded. Week five. Ganga walked with him to the school counsellor's room. "I'll wait outside," she said. Inside, Karthik said it out loud for the first time: "I can't stop the what-ifs." The counsellor listened, then said, "Thank you for telling me. Let's work on this together."

qa.q: What did Karthik drop because his mind wouldn't sit still?
qa.a: Cricket practice.

qa.q: What was Karthik worried about at night in week one?
qa.a: He worried he would fail chemistry, that his headache meant something serious, and that his friends were laughing at him.

qa.q: What turning point came in week five?
qa.a: With Ganga's support, Karthik went to the school counsellor and said the worries out loud for the first time.

qa.q: How might Ganga have felt when Karthik snapped at her?
qa.a: She may have felt hurt at first, but later saw it was part of how tense and sleepless he was.

grounding: It shows a teenager who is tense, sleepless and irritable from constant what-ifs that last and limit his life, and who talks to a counsellor.

passage: "Ojas, you think Bhavna Bua was always this calm? Sit down. When I was sixteen, I couldn't sleep for months. Every night my head ran in circles. What if I fail? What if this cough is something bad? What if my friends secretly hate me? I stopped going to badminton. I snapped at your father, poor boy, over nothing. Everyone said, 'She's just moody. Teenagers.' But it wasn't just moodiness. It went on and on, and my world was getting smaller. My English teacher noticed I'd stopped smiling. She took me to the school counsellor. I was embarrassed. But talking to her, week after week, taught me to catch the what-ifs before they ran away with me. So if your head won't stop at night, beta, don't wait. Tell me. We'll find someone to talk to."

qa.q: What sport did Bhavna Bua stop going to?
qa.a: Badminton.

qa.q: How did Bhavna feel about going to the counsellor at first?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed.

qa.q: What was the turning point for young Bhavna, and why did it help?
qa.a: Her English teacher noticed she had stopped smiling and took her to the school counsellor; talking there week after week taught her to catch the what-ifs.

qa.q: How might the people who called Bhavna 'just moody' have seen her differently?
qa.a: If they had understood, they would have seen a teenager struggling with anxiety that lasted and limited her life, not simple moodiness.

grounding: An aunt recalls her own teenage years of sleeplessness and constant what-ifs that lasted and limited her life, and how talking to a counsellor helped.

passage: At the boarding school, Ishita, fifteen, had not slept properly in five weeks. At lights-out her mind raced: What if I fail chemistry? What if this headache is something serious? What if Riya is angry with me? She checked her marks portal four times a night. In the day she snapped at her roommate for humming and cried in the washroom after a class test. The house mother noticed her dark eyes and walked her to the counsellor, Kamal Sir, that afternoon. Ishita said, "I'm just stressed, like everyone." Kamal Sir listened, then said gently, "Five weeks without sleep and crying every day is bigger than normal exam stress. Let's work on this together." They set a time for the next day, and he called her parents with her.

qa.q: How long had Ishita been sleeping badly?
qa.a: She had not slept properly in five weeks.

qa.q: How was Ishita feeling in the weeks before seeing the counsellor?
qa.a: She felt tense and constantly worried, with racing what-if thoughts, and it showed as irritability and crying.

qa.q: Why was seeing Kamal Sir the right step?
qa.a: The worry had lasted weeks and was limiting her sleep and life, so a counsellor could help, and he involved her parents with her.

qa.q: How might Ishita's roommate have seen her snapping about the humming?
qa.a: The roommate might have felt hurt or confused, not knowing the irritability came from weeks of worry and no sleep.

grounding: Shows a teenager who cannot sleep and spirals over grades, health and friends, seeming irritable, and how lasting worry calls for a counsellor.

passage:
Dear Noor,
I'm sorry I snapped at you on Friday. You didn't deserve it. I want to explain.
For about three months my head hasn't been quiet. At night it runs through lists: what if I fail the unit test, what if my heart is beating weird, what if you and the others are only pretending to like me. I lie awake till two. I check my pulse. Then I'm grumpy all day, and I skip football because I'm too tired.
I thought it was normal nerves. But it's been too long and it's stopping me doing things. So on Monday I went to the school counsellor. It was awkward, but I'm going again Thursday.
I just wanted you to know it wasn't you.
Joseph

qa.q: How long has Joseph's head not been quiet?
qa.a: For about three months.

qa.q: How has Joseph been feeling at night?
qa.a: Joseph has been anxious and tense, lying awake till two with racing what-if thoughts about tests, health and friends.

qa.q: Why did Joseph decide to see the counsellor?
qa.a: Joseph realised it was more than ordinary nerves because it had lasted months and was stopping everyday things like football.

qa.q: How might Noor feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Noor may feel relieved that the snapping wasn't personal, and caring toward Joseph for sharing something hard.

grounding: Shows a teenager tense, sleepless and spiralling about grades, health and friends, seeming irritable, and seeing a counsellor when it lasts and limits life.

passage: Rajni, you asked why I disappeared from the dance group last term. Okay. I'm Deepika, I was fifteen, and I couldn't switch my brain off. Every night: what if I fail maths, what if this cough is serious, what if everyone's talking about me in the group chat? I'd lie there till three, heart thumping. In the mornings I snapped at Mummy over nothing. I stopped going to dance because I was so tired and so sure I'd mess up. I kept telling myself it was just exam stress. But it went on for months. Finally my class teacher noticed and walked me to the school counsellor. Talking to her every week helped me see the loops. I'm back at dance now. That's why.

qa.q: What time would Deepika lie awake until?
qa.a: Deepika would lie awake till three.

qa.q: How was Deepika feeling during those months?
qa.a: Deepika felt tense and anxious, with racing what-ifs, and was irritable and exhausted.

qa.q: What made this more than exam stress, and what helped?
qa.a: It lasted months and stopped Deepika dancing; a class teacher walked Deepika to the school counsellor, and weekly talks helped.

qa.q: How might Rajni have seen Deepika's disappearance from dance?
qa.a: Rajni may have felt confused or hurt, not knowing Deepika was struggling with constant worry.

grounding: Shows a teenager tense, sleepless and spiralling about grades, health and friends, whose lasting worry leads to talking with a counsellor.

passage:
September. Kashish lay awake at one in the morning. What if she failed the chemistry test? What if the headache meant something serious? What if Neha was angry because she hadn't replied? When her mother asked about breakfast, she snapped, "Can everyone just leave me alone?"
October. It hadn't stopped. Kashish quit her dance class because the thought of the recital made her heart race. She sat through lunch without eating, running through what-ifs. Her grades slipped, which gave her new ones.
November. Her friend Neha walked her to Mrs Rukmini, the school counsellor. Kashish told her everything, crying. Mrs Rukmini listened and said this sounded like more than normal exam nerves, since it had gone on for weeks and was stopping her from doing things she loved. They made a plan to meet every week, and to call her parents in together.

qa.q: What class did Kashish quit in October?
qa.a: Her dance class.

qa.q: How was Kashish feeling when she snapped at her mother?
qa.a: She was tense, exhausted from lying awake and overwhelmed by what-if worries, which made her irritable.

qa.q: What was the wise next step for Kashish, and why?
qa.a: Talking to the school counsellor, because the worry had lasted for weeks and was limiting her life, not just ordinary nerves.

qa.q: How might Neha see Kashish's worries in November?
qa.a: Neha seems concerned and caring, noticing her friend was struggling and walking her to someone who could help.

grounding: Kashish's what-if spirals about grades, health and friends last for weeks, cost her sleep and dance, and lead her to a counsellor.
